description.narrative: Jurnalisme Aman (hereafter JA) project aims to create safe and enabling ecosystem for Indonesian journalists to freely conduct their journalistic works and free from the risks of violence and harassments directed towards journalists both offline and online. In the long run, the project aims to also contribute to support free and independent media and journalism in Indonesia. In achieving the objective, the outcome of the project has been twofold: effective complaints-handling mechanisms for journalists established and safety of journalists becomes a priority for all stakeholders. The two strategies aimed to support the digital and physical ecosystem that are safe for journalists in conducting their works.

The document serves as a valuable reference for partners, donors, and media organizations in advancing the program’s impact.

title.narrative: 2024 Report_ Journalist Safety Index 2024Journalist Safety Index:How Do Journalists Survive in an Increasingly Risky Media Landscape?

description.narrative: Freedom of the press is not only a right but also a fundamental pillar of a healthy democracy. Behind every news story, journalists demonstrate dedication in conveying the truth. In Indonesia, however, their reality is far from ideal. Physical threats, legal intimidation, digital attacks, and economic pressures persistently threaten those who speak out.When reporting facts entails significant risk, it is necessary to question whether Indonesia is genuinely a haven for press freedom or a landscape of fear for those committed to truth. Each attack on journalists not only harms individuals but also undermines the democracy that is valued. If journalists are compelled to work in fear, the public's access to honest and balanced information cannot be guaranteed.The 2024 Journalist Safety Index reflects the actual conditions experienced by journalists in Indonesia. Developed through collaboration among the Tifa Foundation, the Nusantara Media Development Association (PPMN), and the Human Rights Working Group (HRWG) within the Safe Journalism consortium, and supported by Populix as a research partner, this report extends beyond statistics. It represents the lived experiences of journalists, highlights the challenges they encounter, and provides a foundation for positive change.This index functions as both a monitoring tool and a basis for developing more effective policies. By mapping diverse risks and protection needs, this report aims to serve as a reference for government, media organizations, and civil society in fostering a safer and more supportive working environment for journalists.Ultimately, press freedom is a right that cannot be disregarded. To achieve a strong and transparent democracy, it is essential to ensure that journalists can work without fear of reprisal. This index marks the beginning of an ongoing effort to establish a more robust protection system for those who are at the forefront of delivering the truth.

title.narrative: Assessment Report on Violence Against Journalists in Three Regions of Indonesia (Aceh, Central Sulawesi, and Southwest Papua)by Tifa Foundation– Project Jurnalisme AmanMapping Across Three Regions: West, Central, and EastCase Studies in the Provinces of Aceh, Central Sulawesi, and Southwest Papua

description.narrative: In the past five years, violence against journalists in Indonesia has increased significantly in frequency, severity, and variety. Journalists are subjected to physical assaults, digital attacks, legal intimidation, criminalization under ambiguous legal provisions, and gender-based harassment. These incidents occur within a broader context of declining civil liberties, inadequate law enforcement, and insufficient institutional protection for media professionals.This report addresses the need for a comprehensive understanding of violence against journalists in Indonesia. Following an initial national assessment in 2023, the current study adopts a more focused approach through case studies in Aceh (West), Central Sulawesi (Central), and Southwest Papua (East). The objective is to systematically map the forms of violence experienced by journalists, analyze their intensity, identify perpetrators, and examine response patterns using both quantitative surveys and qualitative methods, including in-depth interviews and focus group discussions (FGDs).A national survey by the Alliance of Independent Journalists (AJI) involving over 2,000 journalists found that more than 75% of respondents had experienced violence, primarily verbal intimidation, online harassment, or pressure from influential actors. Field studies in Aceh, Central Sulawesi, West Papua, and Southwest Papua demonstrate that violence against journalists frequently occurs in an environment where perpetrators are not held accountable, victims receive minimal support, and media organizations often avoid confrontation instead of protecting their personnel.These findings are reinforced by an evaluation of Indonesia’s legal and institutional frameworks. Although the Press Law normatively guarantees press freedom and journalist protection, in practice, many law enforcement officials—including police, prosecutors, and judges—fail to refer to it when handling journalist-related cases. Conversely, flexible articles within the Electronic Information and Transactions (ITE) Law and the Criminal Code (KUHP) continue to be used to criminalize journalistic work. Memorandums of understanding between the Press Council and security institutions have not been effectively implemented at the local level, while national institutions such as Komdigi and Komnas HAM have yet to play an active role in protecting journalists as part of Indonesia’s human rights agenda.In response to these challenges, journalists and civil society organizations such as AJI, LBH Pers, IJTI, AMSI, and SAFEnet have acted as primary defenders of journalist protection. These organizations offer legal assistance, digital safety training, public advocacy, and collective support, addressing gaps resulting from limited state involvement. However, these efforts are predominantly reactive, limited in reach, and inadequate for establishing a comprehensive and sustainable protection system for journalists.The report reviews international experiences from countries including Colombia, Mexico, Norway, and Sweden as comparative references. These countries have established formal, state-funded mechanisms for journalist protection, coordinated across multiple sectors. Their systems feature national hotlines, emergency evacuation programs, legal and psychosocial support, and mandatory safety training for law enforcement personnel. Recommendations from the UN Plan of Action on the Safety of Journalists and the Issue of Impunity provide further guidance for developing similar policies in Indonesia.This report offers a series of strategic recommendations, including:* Establishing a National Action Plan for Journalist Protection;* Reforming the ITE Law and strengthening the Press Law’s legal standing;* Creating special units within the police and Komdigi;* Allocating budgetary support for victim rehabilitation, and* Integrating press freedom into regional democracy indicators.Journalist protection should be a collective priority for media institutions, professional organizations, civil society, and the state, emphasizing not only response but also prevention and recovery.Journalist safety extends beyond professional concerns and directly affects the public’s right to free and independent information. Democracy depends on a free press, which cannot function amid violence and impunity. Consequently, journalist protection should be recognized as a collective national responsibility rather than a sectoral issue.
